text: Here is a rectangle, forty eight units wide and eighteen tall.
caption: 48 wide, 18 tall

text: We want the greatest common divisor of forty eight and eighteen.
caption: goal: gcd(48, 18)

text: This is the trick Euclid described over two thousand years ago.
The rule is simple: always cut the largest square that fits.
We stop the moment a square uses up what remains exactly.
We will also write the arithmetic down as we go.
Cut an eighteen by eighteen square from the left.
caption: 18 x 18 square

text: A second eighteen by eighteen square fits right beside it.
caption: 18 x 18 square

text: Forty eight splits into two eighteens, with twelve left over.
caption: 48 = 2 x 18 + 12

text: Now cut the largest square that fits: twelve by twelve.
caption: 12 x 12 square

text: Eighteen splits into one twelve, with six left over.
caption: 18 = 1 x 12 + 6

text: Cut a six by six square from the strip.
caption: 6 x 6 square

text: A second six by six square, and nothing is left.
caption: 6 x 6 square

text: Twelve splits into two sixes, with nothing left over.
caption: 12 = 2 x 6 + 0

text: The last square has side six: that is our answer.
caption: gcd = 6

text: Every square we cut traces back to that one number.
Now clear the cuts and look at the rectangle again.
Six by six squares tile it perfectly: eight across, three down.
No gaps, no overlaps, every square lines up exactly.
Try a bigger square and it no longer fits evenly.
The geometry and the arithmetic agree at every single step.
Each step shrinks the numbers fast, so this finishes quickly.
Checking every possible common divisor by hand would take far longer.
That same six also reduces the fraction to eight over three.
One rectangle, a few cuts, and the shared size falls out.
That is the geometry hiding behind the Euclidean algorithm.
